questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes an aldose from a ketose?

options.text: Aldoses contain more carbons
options.misconception: aldose and ketose can have the same count

options.text: The carbonyl is at the end in an aldose and internal in a ketose
Ketoses have no hydroxyl groups
Aldoses are always six-membered rings

questions.explanation: An aldose has a terminal aldehyde carbonyl at carbon one, while a ketose has a ketone carbonyl usually at carbon two; both are polyhydroxy compounds and can form cyclic hemiacetals.
questions.hint: Aldose means aldehyde; ketose means ketone.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: When analyzing the transformation, in a Fischer projection of a sugar, what determines a D configuration?

options.text: The hydroxyl on that carbon is on the left
The carbonyl is at carbon one
options.misconception: that defines an aldose, not D or L

options.text: The hydroxyl on the highest-numbered stereocenter is on the right
The ring is six membered
options.misconception: ring size is not the D/L criterion

questions.explanation: The D or L designation of a sugar is assigned by the position of the hydroxyl on the stereocenter farthest from the carbonyl in a Fischer projection: right means D and left means L.
questions.hint: Look at the lowest chiral carbon in the Fischer projection.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a tutorial session, what molecular process underlies mutarotation of glucose?

options.text: Rotation of the entire molecule in solution
Formation of a glycosidic bond
Oxidation of the aldehyde
Interconversion between alpha and beta anomers through the open-chain form

questions.explanation: Mutarotation is the change in optical rotation as the alpha and beta anomers of a sugar interconvert through the open-chain aldehyde form in solution until an equilibrium mixture is reached.
questions.hint: Anomers interconvert through the open chain.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a glycoside from a hemiacetal
questions.stem: You are given the following: how does a glycoside differ from the cyclic hemiacetal of a sugar?

options.text: The anomeric hydroxyl is replaced by an OR group, forming an acetal
The anomeric carbon bears a hydroxyl
The sugar becomes non-cyclic
The ring oxygen is removed

questions.explanation: A glycoside is an acetal formed when the anomeric hydroxyl of a sugar hemiacetal is replaced by an alkoxy or aryloxy group, locking the anomeric configuration and removing the reducing property.
questions.hint: Glycoside means anomeric acetal.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a synthesis planning session, which structural feature makes a sugar reducing?

options.text: A glycosidic acetal at the anomeric carbon
A free anomeric hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde
The presence of a ketone group
options.misconception: ketoses can be reducing via enediol tautomerization

options.text: A six-membered ring only
options.misconception: ring size is not the criterion

questions.explanation: A sugar is reducing if its anomeric carbon is a hemiacetal that can open to the free carbonyl form, which can then reduce Tollens or Benedict reagents; a glycosidic acetal blocks this.
questions.hint: Free anomeric hemiacetal is required.

provenance.author: orgchem2-bank-author
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A laboratory report asks: which carbons of an aldose are involved in osazone formation with phenylhydrazine?

options.text: Carbons three and four
options.misconception: the reaction occurs at the carbonyl end

options.text: The anomeric carbon only
Carbons one and two
The terminal primary alcohol carbon

questions.explanation: Osazone formation consumes the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent carbon of a reducing sugar, converting both into phenylhydrazone-related groups, so sugars differing only at carbon two give the same osazone.
questions.hint: The first two carbons of the chain react.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For this reaction scenario, what key structural difference distinguishes cellulose from starch?

options.text: Cellulose is made of fructose
Starch contains nitrogen
Cellulose has no glycosidic bonds
Cellulose has beta glycosidic links while starch has alpha links

questions.explanation: Cellulose is a linear polymer of glucose joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds that humans cannot digest, whereas starch contains alpha glycosidic linkages in amylose and amylopectin that human enzymes can hydrolyze.
questions.hint: Alpha versus beta glycosidic links.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In the laboratory (example), what does a Kiliani-Fischer synthesis accomplish?

options.text: It lengthens an aldose chain by one carbon
It shortens the chain by one carbon
It converts an aldose to a ketose
It forms a glycoside

questions.explanation: Kiliani-Fischer synthesis adds a carbon to an aldose chain by forming a cyanohydrin and reducing the nitrile, giving a pair of epimeric aldoses one carbon longer than the starting sugar.
questions.hint: Adds one carbon to the aldose chain.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: What observation indicates a positive Tollens test for a reducing sugar?

options.text: A blue solution turns red
A silver mirror forms on the vessel
A brown precipitate of iodine forms
The solution becomes strongly acidic

questions.explanation: A reducing sugar reduces silver ions in Tollens reagent to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror on the glass; nonreducing sugars such as sucrose give a negative test.
questions.hint: Tollens gives a silver mirror.

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: While planning the experiment, why is fructose, a ketose, still a reducing sugar?

options.text: Ketones always reduce Tollens reagent
Fructose has a free hemiacetal only
It tautomerizes to aldoses under the basic test conditions
The ketose is oxidized directly with no tautomerization

questions.explanation: Under the basic conditions of Tollens or Benedict reagents, fructose undergoes enediol tautomerization to aldoses such as glucose and mannose, which then give a positive reducing test.
questions.hint: Fructose isomerizes to aldoses in base.

questions.stem: A chemist observes the following: how does a glycoside differ from the cyclic hemiacetal of a sugar?

options.text: The anomeric hydroxyl is replaced by an OR group, forming an acetal
The anomeric carbon bears a hydroxyl
The sugar becomes non-cyclic
The ring oxygen is removed

questions.explanation: A glycoside is an acetal formed when the anomeric hydroxyl of a sugar hemiacetal is replaced by an alkoxy or aryloxy group, locking the anomeric configuration and removing the reducing property.
questions.hint: Glycoside means anomeric acetal.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A quiz question asks: which structural feature makes a sugar reducing?

options.text: A glycosidic acetal at the anomeric carbon
A free anomeric hemiacetal that can open to an aldehyde
The presence of a ketone group
options.misconception: ketoses can be reducing via enediol tautomerization

options.text: A six-membered ring only
options.misconception: ring size is not the criterion

questions.explanation: A sugar is reducing if its anomeric carbon is a hemiacetal that can open to the free carbonyl form, which can then reduce Tollens or Benedict reagents; a glycosidic acetal blocks this.
questions.hint: Free anomeric hemiacetal is required.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the sample reaction, which carbons of an aldose are involved in osazone formation with phenylhydrazine?

options.text: Carbons three and four
options.misconception: the reaction occurs at the carbonyl end

options.text: The anomeric carbon only
Carbons one and two
The terminal primary alcohol carbon

questions.explanation: Osazone formation consumes the carbonyl carbon and the adjacent carbon of a reducing sugar, converting both into phenylhydrazone-related groups, so sugars differing only at carbon two give the same osazone.
questions.hint: The first two carbons of the chain react.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: During a lab exercise, what key structural difference distinguishes cellulose from starch?

options.text: Cellulose is made of fructose
Starch contains nitrogen
Cellulose has no glycosidic bonds
Cellulose has beta glycosidic links while starch has alpha links

questions.explanation: Cellulose is a linear polymer of glucose joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds that humans cannot digest, whereas starch contains alpha glycosidic linkages in amylose and amylopectin that human enzymes can hydrolyze.
questions.hint: Alpha versus beta glycosidic links.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In a problem set, what does a Kiliani-Fischer synthesis accomplish?

options.text: It lengthens an aldose chain by one carbon
It shortens the chain by one carbon
It converts an aldose to a ketose
It forms a glycoside

questions.explanation: Kiliani-Fischer synthesis adds a carbon to an aldose chain by forming a cyanohydrin and reducing the nitrile, giving a pair of epimeric aldoses one carbon longer than the starting sugar.
questions.hint: Adds one carbon to the aldose chain.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Testing your understanding: what observation indicates a positive Tollens test for a reducing sugar?

options.text: A blue solution turns red
A silver mirror forms on the vessel
A brown precipitate of iodine forms
The solution becomes strongly acidic

questions.explanation: A reducing sugar reduces silver ions in Tollens reagent to metallic silver, which deposits as a mirror on the glass; nonreducing sugars such as sucrose give a negative test.
questions.hint: Tollens gives a silver mirror.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: A problem asks: why is fructose, a ketose, still a reducing sugar?

options.text: Ketones always reduce Tollens reagent
Fructose has a free hemiacetal only
It tautomerizes to aldoses under the basic test conditions
The ketose is oxidized directly with no tautomerization

questions.explanation: Under the basic conditions of Tollens or Benedict reagents, fructose undergoes enediol tautomerization to aldoses such as glucose and mannose, which then give a positive reducing test.
questions.hint: Fructose isomerizes to aldoses in base.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: For the case in question, which feature distinguishes an aldose from a ketose?

options.text: Aldoses contain more carbons
options.misconception: aldose and ketose can have the same count

options.text: Ketoses have no hydroxyl groups
Aldoses are always six-membered rings
The carbonyl is at the end in an aldose and internal in a ketose

questions.explanation: An aldose has a terminal aldehyde carbonyl at carbon one, while a ketose has a ketone carbonyl usually at carbon two; both are polyhydroxy compounds and can form cyclic hemiacetals.
questions.hint: Aldose means aldehyde; ketose means ketone.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: In class discussion, in a Fischer projection of a sugar, what determines a D configuration?

options.text: The hydroxyl on the highest-numbered stereocenter is on the right
The hydroxyl on that carbon is on the left
The carbonyl is at carbon one
options.misconception: that defines an aldose, not D or L

options.text: The ring is six membered
options.misconception: ring size is not the D/L criterion

questions.explanation: The D or L designation of a sugar is assigned by the position of the hydroxyl on the stereocenter farthest from the carbonyl in a Fischer projection: right means D and left means L.
questions.hint: Look at the lowest chiral carbon in the Fischer projection.

questions.subject: ORGANIC_CHEMISTRY_II
questions.stem: Working through the mechanism, what molecular process underlies mutarotation of glucose?

options.text: Rotation of the entire molecule in solution
Interconversion between alpha and beta anomers through the open-chain form
Formation of a glycosidic bond
Oxidation of the aldehyde

questions.explanation: Mutarotation is the change in optical rotation as the alpha and beta anomers of a sugar interconvert through the open-chain aldehyde form in solution until an equilibrium mixture is reached.
questions.hint: Anomers interconvert through the open chain.
